topics.summary: How 21 countries share one currency: who runs it, the rules for joining, the 2 percent goal, and how inflation, growth and government debt are read across the bloc.

cards.title: One Currency, Many Countries
cards.definition: The euro is a single currency shared by a group of European Union members called the euro area or eurozone. Each country keeps its own government, budget and taxes, but gives up its own currency and interest rate. Monetary policy for the whole area is set centrally, so the same interest rate applies whether a member's economy is booming or shrinking.
cards.example: The euro was launched on 1 January 1999 for accounting and electronic payments, and notes and coins followed on 1 January 2002. By 2026, 21 of the 27 EU countries used it, with Bulgaria the latest to join, and some 358 million people paid with euro cash every day.

cards.title: The Eurosystem
cards.definition: The European System of Central Banks is the European Central Bank plus the national central banks of every EU member, whether or not it uses the euro. The Eurosystem is the smaller group: the ECB plus the national central banks of euro countries. The Eurosystem runs the single monetary policy, with the ECB at its core and national banks carrying out operations locally.
cards.example: The ECB has set monetary policy for the euro area since January 1999. Eleven countries started; Greece joined in 2001, Slovenia in 2007, Cyprus and Malta in 2008, Slovakia in 2009, Estonia in 2011, Latvia in 2014, Lithuania in 2015, Croatia in 2023 and Bulgaria in 2026.

cards.title: The Rules for Joining
cards.definition: Before a country can adopt the euro it must meet convergence criteria written into the EU Treaty. The idea is that economies sharing one interest rate should already look alike: low inflation, sound public finances, a stable exchange rate and long-term interest rates close to the best performers. The criteria are tested when a country applies for membership, not enforced afterwards, which is one reason the tests are strict.
cards.example: The tests: inflation no more than 1.5 percentage points above the average of the 3 lowest-inflation members; a government deficit within 3 percent of GDP and debt within 60 percent of GDP; at least 2 years in the exchange rate mechanism without devaluing; and long-term rates no more than 2 percentage points above the 3 best performers.

cards.title: Price Stability at 2 Percent
cards.definition: The Treaty makes price stability the ECB's primary objective but does not define it. The ECB does. After its 2021 strategy review it set a target of 2 percent inflation over the medium term and made the target symmetric, meaning undershooting is as unwelcome as overshooting. The target applies to the euro area as a whole, not to each member separately.
cards.example: The Governing Council adopted the 2 percent symmetric target in July 2021. It measures inflation with the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, a basket built the same way in every member so that a 2 percent reading in one country means the same as in another. Medium term means the ECB does not react to every month's wobble.

cards.title: Reading an Inflation Flash
cards.definition: A flash estimate is an early reading of inflation published within days of the month's end, before all the data are in. It breaks the headline into components: energy, food, industrial goods and services. Watching the pieces matters because a jump driven by energy can reverse quickly, while services inflation tends to move slowly and reflects wages. The full figure follows about two weeks later.
cards.example: Eurostat's flash estimate of September 1, 2026 put euro area annual inflation at 3.3 percent for August 2026, up from 2.9 percent in July. Energy ran at 14.3 percent, up from 10.3 percent; services eased to 3.0 percent from 3.3 percent; non-energy industrial goods were 1.2 percent and food, alcohol and tobacco 1.2 percent.

cards.definition: Eurostat reports euro area GDP two ways: the change from the previous quarter, which shows momentum, and the change from a year earlier, which smooths out seasonal quirks. It publishes employment alongside, because output can grow while jobs stall if productivity rises. The EU total is larger than the euro area total since it also includes the 6 members that do not use the euro.

cards.title: Government Debt in a Currency Union
cards.definition: Euro members share a currency but each issues its own government debt and has its own budget; there is no common treasury standing behind them. That is why debt ratios matter so much in the euro area: a member with heavy debt cannot print its way out, and its bonds trade at rates that reflect its own finances rather than the bloc's.
cards.example: At the end of the first quarter of 2026 euro area government debt was 88.9 percent of GDP, up from 87.2 percent a year earlier. Greece stood at 143.5 percent, Italy 138.9 percent and France 117.6 percent; Estonia was lowest at 25.2 percent. Of the total, 84.3 percent was debt securities, 13.2 percent loans and 2.5 percent currency and deposits.

cards.title: Exchange Rates Fixed Forever
cards.definition: Joining the euro means converting a national currency at a rate fixed irrevocably; the old currency then ceases to exist. Unlike a peg, which a government can abandon under pressure, the conversion rate has no exit. That permanence is what gives the union credibility, and also why the convergence tests come before entry: once in, a country can no longer devalue.

Belgium and 10 other founders locked theirs on 1 January 1999, at 40.3399 Belgian francs per euro for example, and used the new notes from 2002. cards.title: China's Economy in 2025
cards.definition: China measures its output the way other countries do, as gross domestic product, and publishes a preliminary annual figure in January. Growth is reported in real terms, after removing price changes, against the same period a year earlier. Because the quarterly readings are year-on-year, a slowing quarterly sequence within a year signals a loss of momentum even when the annual total looks steady.
cards.example: GDP in 2025 was 140,187.9 billion yuan, about 140.2 trillion yuan, up 5.0 percent on 2024, according to the preliminary accounting released January 21, 2026. The quarters slowed through the year: 5.4 percent, 5.2 percent, 4.8 percent and 4.5 percent year on year.

cards.title: Four Decades of Catch-up
cards.definition: Economic reform in China began in 1978, opening the economy to markets and trade. The result was one of the fastest sustained expansions on record, which moved the country through the World Bank's income groups and pulled hundreds of millions of people above the extreme poverty line. The pace has slowed as the population ages and the easy gains from moving farm workers into factories have been taken.
cards.example: GDP growth averaged more than 9 percent a year from 1978 into the 2020s, and almost 800 million people were lifted out of extreme poverty. China moved from the low-income group to the upper-middle-income group. The World Bank's 2026 update projected growth easing to 4.4 percent in 2026 as aging and weaker demand weigh.

cards.title: A Population That Is Shrinking
cards.definition: A population shrinks when deaths outnumber births and migration does not fill the gap. For an economy that means fewer new workers each year and more retirees per worker, which weighs on growth and public finances. Urbanization, the share of people living in cities, can still rise even as the total falls, because people keep moving from countryside to town.
cards.example: At the end of 2025 China's population was 1,404.89 million, down 3.39 million over the year, with 7.92 million births against 11.31 million deaths. The urbanization rate rose 0.89 percentage points to 67.89 percent, according to the statistical communiqué of February 28, 2026.

cards.title: Three Sectors
cards.definition: Statisticians split an economy into primary industry (farming, forestry, fishing), secondary industry (manufacturing, mining, construction) and tertiary industry (services). As economies mature, services grow fastest and take the largest share. China's figures show that shift under way, with construction, long a growth engine, contracting even as services expanded. Watching the three sectors separately shows where growth is actually coming from, which a single GDP number hides.

cards.title: Household Income and Spending
cards.definition: Per capita disposable income is what the average person has left to spend or save after taxes and transfers. Retail sales measure what households actually buy. Comparing the two with consumer prices shows whether living standards are rising: if income grows faster than prices, real purchasing power increases. A flat price index means every yuan of extra income was real.

cards.title: A Managed Float
cards.definition: A managed floating exchange rate lets the currency move with market supply and demand inside limits set by the central bank. China's version references a basket of currencies rather than the U.S. dollar alone, and the central bank publishes a daily central parity around which trading may move within a band. It is neither a hard peg nor a free float.
cards.example: China unified its dual exchange rates on January 1, 1994 and on July 21, 2005 moved to a managed float based on market supply and demand with reference to a basket of currencies. The daily band against the dollar was 0.3 percent at the 2005 reform and was widened to 0.5 percent in 2007.

cards.title: Tools of the People's Bank
cards.definition: The People's Bank of China steers credit with several levers. The required reserve ratio sets how much of their deposits banks must park at the central bank; cutting it frees money to lend. The 7-day reverse repo rate is the short-term policy rate. The loan prime rate is the benchmark banks quote to their best customers, and it guides mortgage and business loan pricing.
cards.example: The 7-day reverse repo rate was designated the policy rate in July 2024. Over the 2021 to 2025 plan period the reserve ratio was cut 9 times, by 3.5 percentage points in total, releasing about 7 trillion yuan of long-term liquidity, and the 1-year loan prime rate fell 0.85 percentage points. cards.title: Big Economy, Middle Income
cards.definition: Total GDP and GDP per person tell different stories. A country can have the second-largest economy in the world and still have an average income well below that of rich countries, simply because the output is shared among many more people. Per capita figures are what matter for living standards; totals are what matter for the country's weight in world trade and finance.

cards.title: What "Emerging Market" Means
cards.definition: There is no single official definition of an emerging market. The phrase usually means a middle-income economy that is growing and opening to trade and investment but whose financial markets are smaller and less developed than those of rich countries. The World Bank avoids the label and instead sorts every economy into 4 income groups by national income per person.
cards.example: The World Bank groups economies as low, lower-middle, upper-middle or high income using gross national income per capita converted with its Atlas method, updated every July 1. In the classification announced in July 2022, low income meant $1,085 or less per person and lower-middle income ran from $1,086 to $4,255.

cards.title: Extreme Poverty
cards.definition: Extreme poverty is living below an international poverty line that the World Bank sets in purchasing-power terms, so that a dollar buys the same basket in every country. The line is revised as price data improve. Falling poverty in East and South Asia drove most of the decline since 1990; what remains is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and in places affected by conflict.
cards.example: The international line is $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing-power parity. In the World Bank's 2025 estimates about 831 million people lived below it, down from roughly 2.3 billion in 1990. An estimated 412 million children aged 17 or under lived in such households in 2024, and progress has slowed over the past decade.

cards.title: Remittances
cards.definition: Remittances are money that migrants send home to family. For many developing countries they are a larger and steadier source of foreign currency than investment by foreign firms or aid from governments, because migrants keep sending even when the home economy is weak. The cost of sending money matters: every percentage point of fees is income that never arrives, which is why lowering that cost is a development goal in itself.
cards.example: Remittances to low- and middle-income countries reached $669 billion in 2023, up 3.8 percent, and exceeded foreign direct investment and official aid combined. The largest recipients were India at $125 billion, Mexico $67 billion, China $50 billion, the Philippines $40 billion and Egypt $24 billion. Sending $200 cost 6.2 percent on average in the second quarter of 2023.

cards.title: Foreign Direct Investment
cards.definition: Foreign direct investment is money a company puts into a lasting stake abroad: a factory, a mine, a subsidiary. It brings capital, technology and jobs and is harder to withdraw than a bond or a bank loan. Headline totals can mislead, because some flows merely pass through low-tax conduit economies on their way elsewhere without building anything, so analysts strip those out.

Flows to developed economies dropped 22 percent, with Europe down 58 percent. Developing economies were broadly stable: Southeast Asia rose 10 percent to $225 billion while Latin America fell 12 percent, and project finance dropped 26 percent.

cards.title: Borrowing in Someone Else's Currency
cards.definition: When a country borrows in a foreign currency at a floating interest rate, it takes on two risks it cannot control: the lender's central bank can raise rates, and its own currency can fall, making each repayment cost more at home. In the 1970s banks recycled oil exporters' surplus dollars into loans to Latin America on exactly those terms, and cheap real rates made the debt seem manageable.
cards.example: Latin American debt rose from $29 billion in 1970 to $159 billion in 1978 and $327 billion in 1982. When the United States tightened money to fight inflation, rates jumped and repayment periods shortened. In August 1982 Mexico announced it could not service its $80 billion debt; 16 Latin American countries and 11 others went on to reschedule.

cards.title: The Lost Decade and the Brady Plan
cards.definition: A debt crisis becomes a lost decade when the cure, austerity to keep paying, chokes growth for years. Debt reduction breaks the cycle by writing part of the debt off in exchange for new bonds the borrower can service. Lenders accept a loss because a smaller debt that gets paid is worth more than a larger one that does not. Regulators first had to be sure the banks could absorb the write-offs.
cards.example: By 1982 the 9 largest U.S. banks held Latin American debt equal to 176 percent of their capital. The years 1982 to 1989 brought high unemployment, falling incomes per person and stagnant growth. The Brady plan of 1989 offered permanent relief: between 1989 and 1994 private lenders forgave $61 billion, about one-third of the debt.

cards.title: When a Peg Breaks: Asia, 1997
cards.definition: A currency peg fixes the exchange rate to the dollar. It invites firms and banks to borrow in dollars, often short term, because the rate seems guaranteed. If foreign lenders lose confidence and pull out, the central bank runs short of reserves and the peg breaks. The currency falls, and every dollar debt suddenly costs far more in local money, pushing borrowers into insolvency.
cards.example: On July 2, 1997 Thailand devalued its currency against the dollar, and the crisis spread to Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Hong Kong and South Korea through December 1998. Firms saw the local value of their foreign debts jump. The IMF, World Bank, Asian Development Bank and governments mobilized $118 billion for Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea, with reforms as conditions.

cards.title: Spillovers to the Rest of the World
cards.definition: A crisis in emerging markets travels along two channels. Trade: collapsing demand and cheaper currencies mean cheaper exports, which lowers prices elsewhere. Finance: investors flee to the safest assets, usually U.S. Treasury bonds, pushing their yields down. So the same shock that devastates the crisis countries can arrive in rich economies as lower inflation and cheaper borrowing, at least at first.
cards.example: Before 1997 the affected Asian economies had grown 5 to 10 percent a year, which masked heavy short-term foreign borrowing and weak supervision. After July 1997 capital inflows slowed or reversed and several countries fell into deep recession, while the United States saw reduced inflation pressure from cheaper Asian imports and weaker commodity prices, and lower bond yields as money sought dollar assets.
